Great guy. I would qualify one point, though. Europe has more than done its bit in innovation, particularly in engineering, manufacturing and retail. It's a mature economic landscape, much like the US, but approaches innovation through a different lens and again that I think is attributed to its culture just like it is in the US.

India, on the other hand, is still a developing economy. It will naturally draw water from the pool closest to it rather than venture to the edge. And that pool is its enormous, still-maturing consumer market. Much of India's innovation is therefore focused on using existing technology to make that market more efficient, whether by borrowing ideas from developed economies or solving problems unique to India. That doesn't necessarily reflect a lack of innovation or risk appetite. It reflects where the economic opportunities currently lie.

As for AI, we are looking at an expanding circle moving in every direction. It needs a vaccine to limit the harm it can cause and nutrition to nurture the good it can do. Eventually, the hype surrounding this circle will flatten out. That is when we will get a clearer picture of its true economic value.

And yes, as the wise man rightly says, diversify your risk -  a simple first principle, particularly when nobody really knows how this will play out.

Those questioning Damodaran Sir for valuing Zomato at ₹40 in 2021 need to understand one thing: Blinkit wasn't even part of Zomato back then. Zomato acquired Blinkit in 2022.

Today, Blinkit contributes approximately 78 to 
 80% of Eternal's revenue.

Comparing 2021 Zomato with today's Eternal without considering this acquisition is misleading.

Before questioning a legend, understand the valuation date, market conditions, assumptions and parameters considered at that time.

Valuations can be wrong, but criticism without research is even worse. Respect the process, then question the outcome.
